The mridangam is a membranophone from southern India, traditionally associated with the Tamil Nadu region, and the main rhythmic accompaniment of Carnatic music. Its body is usually hollowed from jackwood, with heads of sheep, cow or buffalo hide at both ends, tensioned with leather straps; the two faces differ in diameter, the smaller giving the high sound and the larger the low. The percussionist produces the rhythm by striking, often with the ghatam, the kanjira, the morsing and other percussion instruments, and it can also be played solo.
姆裡丹加鼓為膜鳴樂器，演奏前需先調音：將鼓直立、較大鼓面朝下，以重物敲擊小鼓面周: The mridangam is a membranophone, and it has to be tuned before playing: stand the drum upright with the larger head down and tap the leather straps around the small head with a heavy object — tapping towards the body raises the pitch and tapping the other way lowers it; on modern instruments fixed with nuts a wrench is used. Before a performance the leather of the large head is usually damped and a little paste of coarse wheat flour and water is put in the centre, which lowers the pitch and strengthens the bass. A beginner can first get the two faces to speak: the small head gives a higher, metallic sound and the large head a lower one; when tuning, the pitch around the edge of the small head has to be even, and a pitch pipe or a tambura can be used to check it.

Both openings are covered with sheep, cow or buffalo hide, tensioned with leather thongs that run along the body. The centre of the smaller head carries a tuning paste, which the source gives as rice flour, iron oxide powder and starch; another source records that the black paste contains clay particles and rice. Before playing, the wide leather head is damped and coarse wheat flour and water are put in the centre, and a rubber paste is also used today. Some modern heads are fixed with nuts and bolts.
姆裡丹加鼓起源於印度次大陸，早期與陶泥有關，後以菠蘿蜜木製成；在南印度坦米爾文化: The mridangam originated in the Indian subcontinent; early instruments were connected with clay, and later ones were made of jackwood. In Tamil culture in South India it is called the tannumai, and it appears in Sangam literature, the Natya Shastra and the Silappatikaram. It was at first an ensemble instrument for the court, for war and for the prelude to drama, and later became the main rhythmic accompaniment of Carnatic music and developed a solo role; its development went with the tala rhythmic system, and it is related to the pakhawaj, the tabla and the Southeast Asian kendang.
姆裡丹加鼓音色溫潤而富有層次感，既不失明亮的穿透力，又帶有深沉的共鳴特質。其雙面: The mridangam's timbre is warm and full of layers, keeping a bright penetration while also having a deep resonance. Its two heads let it produce a range that runs between high and low, the bass heavy and strong, the treble clear and nimble, so the instrument spans a wide compass. The body resonates well, and each stroke sets off a deep harmonic ring, making a warm and resonant sound. Beside the ghatam the mridangam sounds more refined and finely shaded; beside the kanjira its volume is heavier and fuller. Its tone combines rhythmic precision with richness of colour, so that in South Indian classical music it can hold the accompaniment steady without losing expressiveness.
